part_title: QuickSight Security, Cross-Region Access and User Management

scenes.title: QuickSight account access
scenes.narration: This diagram separates a person's sign-in from the data they may see. Start with users authenticating through IAM Identity Center or a corporate identity provider. QuickSight maps the authenticated user into its configured account, namespace and role, such as Reader, Author or Admin. A Reader explores shared dashboards but does not create and publish analyses like an Author. An Admin has additional account and user-management capabilities. The two namespace columns illustrate how QuickSight can organise separate groups of users. But here is the important distinction: a QuickSight role controls capabilities inside QuickSight; it does not automatically grant the service access to every S3, Athena or Redshift dataset. That second trust boundary requires appropriate data-resource permissions and, for some sources, network connectivity. Follow the bottom two steps: authenticate the user, then separately authorise data access. For a GenAI operations dashboard, a person who may view performance metrics should not necessarily see raw customer prompts or another department's financial data. Build least-privilege access in both layers.

scenes.title: QuickSight resource access
scenes.narration: This slide shows QuickSight reaching AWS data sources through explicitly permitted paths. The analyst opens a QuickSight dashboard; QuickSight uses an appropriate service role and configured data-source identity to query Athena, read approved S3 objects or connect to Redshift. The example policy panels list Athena query operations, an S3 object-resource permission and Redshift connection or credential actions. On the blocked side, DynamoDB has no matching authorised path, demonstrating default denial. Be careful with the precise policy details. A service role, S3 bucket policy, workgroup settings, KMS key policy and database permissions may all participate, depending on the source. Granting IAM GetObject is not the same as giving database SELECT access. Likewise, simply naming the QuickSight service principal in a bucket policy without restricting the intended account and resource context may be too broad. When a dataset refuses to refresh, inspect the identity performing the request and the complete resource policy chain. Use explicit authorised resources, not a wildcard AdministratorAccess workaround.

scenes.title: QuickSight cross-region access
scenes.narration: The diagram places QuickSight in Region A and Redshift or RDS data in Region B. Follow the request: QuickSight connects over a supported network path, authenticates to the source using its configured permissions, queries the data and receives results in the QuickSight Region. The connection options include an approved public endpoint with TLS or compatible private network connectivity. Do not assume that every QuickSight data-source connection can use any PrivateLink endpoint automatically; supported VPC connection configurations, routing, endpoints and Regions need checking for the actual data source. The lower comparison calls out two operational consequences: cross-Region traffic adds latency and can introduce inter-Region transfer charges. For an interactive dashboard, that extra round trip may become noticeable when every filter triggers a new live query. Consider SPICE import with a suitable refresh cadence, or a local reporting replica, when data freshness and cost requirements allow. Access across Regions also requires verifying the source database credentials, network security groups, IAM roles and encryption controls. A working connection is not automatic permission to every table.

scenes.title: QuickSight Cross-Account Connectivity
scenes.narration: Here the important boundary is between an analytics account and a producer account. Follow the analyst to QuickSight in the analytics account. The intended cross-account access path uses an IAM role or data-source identity that is trusted and permitted to access selected producer resources. On the provider side, resource policies and relevant grants allow just the approved S3 objects, warehouse data or other supported source. Data is then returned to the analytics environment for authorised datasets and dashboards. The diagram simplifies several AWS mechanisms into one flow, so remember that QuickSight does not magically assume an arbitrary cross-account role for every connection type. The actual trust, identity propagation and resource policy must match the supported integration. For S3, both the identity's permissions and the bucket or KMS policies may matter. For a database, network connectivity and database-level privileges are also required. Test access using the same effective service identity as the real dataset. Cross-account trust should expose only the curated data required for analysis, not the entire producer account.

scenes.title: QuickSight user management
scenes.narration: This slide begins with QuickSight users and groups, then shows how Readers, Authors and Admins use different features. Readers consume permitted dashboards, Authors build analyses and publish dashboards, and Admins manage the environment. Next, look at the sample dashboard and dataset containing regional sales records for the US, EMEA and APAC. Row-level security rules restrict which records are visible based on the user's or group's authorised region. A US salesperson should not retrieve APAC records just by changing a filter in the visual. The example also includes executives with broader legitimate business access, showing why permissions depend on role and responsibility. It is important to distinguish QuickSight membership from data-level filtering: a shared dashboard alone is not enough to enforce tenant isolation. Define and test row-level security at the dataset layer, and consider column-level security for sensitive fields. If a user's assigned region changes, update the underlying access mapping and verify the results. Effective BI security protects both who may open a dashboard and which underlying records they may query.
